title: Floquet spintronics: tuning the current-induced spin polarization of topological surface states with light
authors: Youngjae Kim, Aayushi Agrawal, Kwon Park
abstract: Topological surface states are a promising platform for spintronics due to spin-momentum locking. Spin-momentum locking can induce a net spin polarization in topological surface states via an electric current, a phenomenon known as the Edelstein effect. In this work, using Floquet theory, we show that the current-induced spin polarization of topological surface states can be tuned by illuminating them with light, thereby modifying their spin texture in momentum space. Specifically, the electric spin susceptibility of topological surface states can be controlled and even reversed by varying the electric-field strength of high-frequency, circularly polarized light.
summary: The paper introduces 'Floquet spintronics' by theoretically showing that illuminating topological surface states with high-frequency light allows for the active tuning and reversal of the current-induced spin polarization. By applying Floquet theory to the system Hamiltonian, the authors predict measurable sign changes in the electric spin susceptibility as a function of the driving field strength.
main_problem: The work aims to demonstrate that the spin polarization induced by an electric current in topological surface states can be actively tuned and even reversed using external high-frequency, circularly polarized light.
main_result: The transverse electric spin susceptibilities ($\chi^s_{xy}, \chi^s_{yx}$) exhibit a sign change as the light field strength is varied, confirming that the current-induced spin polarization can be controlled by Floquet driving.
method: The study employs Floquet theory to analyze the time-periodic Hamiltonian and calculates observables using generalized Kubo formulas derived from Floquet eigenstates.
model_or_system: The physical system is modeled as topological surface states (e.g., in $	ext{Bi}_2	ext{Se}_3$) subjected to a time-dependent electromagnetic field, leading to the use of a Floquet Hamiltonian approach.
key_observables: Electric spin susceptibility ($\chi^s_{\alpha eta}$), spin texture components ($s(\mathbf{k})$), and Berry curvature $F(\mathbf{k})$.
important_parameters: Normalized electric-field strength ($A$) of the circularly polarized light, and the high-frequency limit ($\Omega \gg$ energy gaps).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation via Floquet theory, assuming a high-frequency regime for the driving field.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the Edelstein effect and its control by light. Figure 2 plots $\chi^s$ vs. $A$, showing sign changes in transverse components. Figures 3 and 4 track spin texture evolution and Berry curvature changes across critical values of $A$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the high-frequency effective Hamiltonian using the Floquet-Magnus expansion, derives this effective Hamiltonian, and then uses it to calculate the electric spin susceptibility, demonstrating the sign reversal as a function of light intensity.
why_interesting: This work directly bridges concepts from quantum optics (Floquet engineering) with condensed matter spintronics, showing how external fields can manipulate intrinsic electronic properties like spin polarization in topological materials.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic illustration for Floquet spintronics using topological surface states. (a) A net spin polariza- tion can be induced in topological surface states by an electric current, a phenomenon known as the Edelstein effect. (b) The electric spin polarization can be controlled and even reversed at sufficiently strong electric-field strength of high-frequency, circularly polarized light, which would open a new frontier in Floquet engineering, namely Floquet spintronics.

FIG. 2. Electric spin susceptibility. The electric spin sus- ceptibility is plotted as a function of the normalized electric- field strength A of high-frequency, circularly polarized light. Here, A = eE0a/ℏΩ, where e is the electron charge, E0 is the electric-field strength, a is the lattice constant, and Ωis the light frequency. Throughout this work, the light frequency Ω is set to 8 eV, which is 1,000 times the minimum energy gap of the quasienergy bands. (a) Transverse electric spin suscep- tibilities, χs xy and χs yx, as a function of A. (b) Longitudinal electric spin susceptibilities, χs xx and χs yy, as a function of A. FIG. 3. Minimum energy gap and evolution of spin texture. (a) Minimum energy gap ∆min as a function of the normalized electric-field strength A of high-frequency, circularly polarized light. (b) In-plane components of the spin texture in momentum space, s∥(k), for the conduction band at different values of A, indicated by the following symbols: (i) triangle, A = 0; (ii) square, A = 1.65; (iii) star, A = 1.88; (iv) David’s star, A = 1.98; (v) pentagon, A = 2.05; and (vi) hexagon, A = 2.81. Note that the positions of the minimum energy gap are indicated by solid white circles.

FIG. 4. Berry curvature and topological phase transitions. The Berry curvature F is plotted as a function of the normalized electric-field strength A of high-frequency, circularly polarized light. (a) The Berry curvature exhibits sharp peaks at the positions of the minimum energy gap in the absence of illumination, i.e., at A = 0. (b) The Berry curvature becomes predominantly positive at A = 1.65. (c) The Berry curvature remains overall positive, but negative regions grow at A = 1.88. (d) The Berry curvature becomes predominantly negative at A = 1.98.
